The Civil Rights Act of Nineteen Sixty-Four. A landmark federal law passed by the United States Congress, the Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four prohibited discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson, it was the most comprehensive civil rights legislation in American history, outlawing segregation in public accommodations—hotels, restaurants, theaters—mandating school desegregation, protecting voting rights, and establishing the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to combat workplace discrimination. The Act represented the culmination of the Civil Rights Movement's nonviolent direct action campaign and fundamentally transformed American law and society.

The Act was introduced by President Lyndon B. Johnson following the assassination of President John F. Kennedy and the historic March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in nineteen sixty-three, where Martin Luther King Junior delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech. Title Two of the Act prohibited discrimination in public accommodations—hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other businesses offering services to the public—a direct response to sit-in campaigns that had challenged segregation in the South.

Title Three authorized the federal government and the Attorney General to initiate litigation to desegregate public schools, providing federal enforcement power for school integration previously required by the Brown versus Board of Education decision in nineteen fifty-four. Title Six cut off federal funding to any institution or program practicing discrimination, giving federal agencies powerful leverage to enforce desegregation in schools, hospitals, and other federally-funded institutions. Title Seven established the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to investigate complaints of employment discrimination and enforce prohibitions against discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

The Act mandated the collection of voting statistics to document racial discrimination in voter registration, supporting the subsequent Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five. The Act's passage required overcoming a Southern Democratic filibuster in the Senate, with Senate Majority Leader Hubert Humphrey and Republican Senator Everett Dirksen building a cross-party coalition to secure the necessary votes. Title Nine, added in nineteen seventy-two, extended the Act's prohibition of discrimination to education, mandating equality in school athletics and academic programs, becoming the foundation for gender equality in sports.

The Act's passage represented a pivotal moment in the Civil Rights Movement, validating the strategy of nonviolent direct action and legislative advocacy pursued by Martin Luther King Junior and others. Enforcement of the Act was uneven and contested: Southern states and private individuals resisted integration through massive resistance campaigns, and subsequent court decisions narrowed some of the Act's protections, but it remained foundational to American civil rights law.
